title: JSON by concatenation

blocks.text: The page's first example is a small JSON object built from traditional literals joined with `+`. Each source line needs its own `\n`, and the page's pitfall shows what a missing one does: `"SELECT *" + "FROM users"` becomes `SELECT *FROM users`.
Write `UserJson.of(String name, int age)`. It returns exactly these four lines, joined by `\n`, with no newline after the last one:
The inner lines are indented by four spaces. `name` is written as a JSON string, so a double quote inside it is written `\"` and a backslash `\\`.
(`/` separates the lines here; the answer joins them with `\n`.)

cases.says: The JSON has its four lines, indented as shown, with no newline after the closing brace.
A double quote inside the name is written \" so the JSON string stays closed.
A backslash inside the name is written \\ for JSON, before any quote is escaped.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: A concatenated piece that lacks its \n glues onto the next line, as in SELECT *FROM users.
A traditional literal cannot span source lines, so a multi-line value is built from pieces joined with + and explicit \n.
